items.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It was McCoy Tyner, so we got him.

ctx.x: That’s about it. I think he might have played a couple one-nighters someplace, which I couldn’t make ‘cause I was working on something else when the dates came up, but we made a couple records for ABC Paramount. That was about it. Benny and I would run into each other on various situations, and then finally when I left Mulligan when Mulligan was organizing the Concert Jazz Band or Orchestra, then I’m thinking I would like to start a group again. I was thinking I was gonna call Benny and ask him would he be…

“Just bring me a bottle of Scotch. Dewar’s will be okay.” That’s nothing, but that was McCoy’s introduction to the jazz audience other than playing in Philadelphia. Now, it would’ve happened sooner than later anyway, but we were fortunate to have him because McCoy was McCoy.

items.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Benny wanted me to join this band he was forming with Art Farmer which became the Jazztet.

ctx.x: Got your diploma from West Philly? So if you were born in ‘38 that would put you at about, ‘56 you’re probably getting out of high school or just finishing if you graduated when you were eighteen-although you were born in December so it might have been more in ’57 when you graduated from high school. What were your goals at that point?

I just wanted to continue my music, continue my music career, because I had already kind of established my name with some guys and Benny wanted me to join this band he was forming with Art Farmer which became the Jazztet. John hadn’t left Miles yet, I think he was

planning to and he wanted me to be in his band, so I was kind of torn between the two. I think I worked with Jazztet and we did “Killer Joe” and all those numbers. Then I told Benny, “Look, John has asked me to join his band.” Naima, John’s wife at the time was good friends with my wife.
